title.narrative: United Nations Central Emergency Response Fund (CERF) core contributions 2022-2026 (Global)

description.narrative: The Australia – UN Central Emergency Response Fund (CERF) Strategic Partnership Framework (SPF) sets the objectives and obligations for the partnership. It outlines the parameters for Australia's global funding, and the requirements for any subsidiary arrangements that will direct funding to specific funding windows.

organisation.narrative: Australia - Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade

description.narrative: Australia’s funding to CERF provides life-saving humanitarian relief to civilians affected by armed conflict. CERF allocated over half of its annual funding – $372 million – to assist almost 12.1 million conflict-affected people. Most ($177 million, or 48 per cent) was allocated in response to conflict-related internal displacement, reaching over 5 million people. In Ukraine, CERF allocated $20.5 million within hours of the outbreak of full-scale war, helping partners to provide much-needed assistance, such as shelter and protection. CERF later allocated another $40 million, providing nearly 1 million people with access to water and daily essentials at places of refuge.

CERF continues to support scaling up of anticipatory action to ensure a more efficient, effective and dignified humanitarian response. CERF also uses early action allocations to enhance the timeliness and impact of humanitarian assistance. In 2023, CERF was forward leaning by increasing funding for early action, based on forecasts, to ensure people exposed to crises received assistance as early as possible. In 2023, CERF provided USD 124 million for early action to get ahead of rising food insecurity, disease outbreaks, flooding and drought, including events driven by El Niño – assisting around 3.8 million people in 10 countries. Some USD 1.7 million of Australia’s 2023 contribution to CERF can be attributed to advancing anticipatory action and early action and contributed to assist 56,000 people.

In 2024, the Central Emergency Response Fund (CERF) expanded its anticipatory action activities to 20 countries, and allocated around $123 million to reduce the effects of predictable crises. This enabled 17 countries to develop frameworks incorporating predictive analytics, pre-agreed interventions, and rapid funding mechanisms to support timely and effective future responses. ‍ In July 2024, CERF provided anticipatory funding to WFP, UNICEF, UNFPA, and FAO in Bangladesh ahead of severe monsoon flooding in the Jamuna Basin. This early intervention, through local partners, helped 388,000 people across five vulnerable districts access multi-purpose cash, WASH, and sexual and reproductive health support, enabling communities to secure food, protect livestock, and recover more quickly. ‍ The approach proved more cost-effective and dignified than reactive responses, with an emphasis on preparedness, local engagement, and evidence-based decision-making.
